content: Moisturizers, also spelled as moisturisers, are intricate formulations of chemical agents specifically designed to enhance the softness and flexibility of the outermost layers of the skin, known as the epidermis. This is achieved by increasing the skin's hydration levels, or water content. These products may contain naturally occurring skin lipids and sterols, as well as synthetic or natural oils, humectants, emollients, and lubricants, among other components. Commercially available moisturizers are widely used for both cosmetic and therapeutic purposes. However, they can also be prepared at home using common pharmaceutical ingredients. Beyond their primary function of restoring or maintaining normal hydration levels in the skin, moisturizers can provide additional benefits. These include forming a protective barrier to prevent water loss through the epidermis, repairing dry, scaly, or damaged skin caused by environmental factors or internal conditions (such as acne or naturally dry skin), and mitigating or delaying the visible effects of skin aging. While simple and effective moisturizers can be made using just a few basic ingredients, such as stearate, olive oil, water, and glycerin, commercial formulations are often highly complex and diverse in composition. These may include: Humectants: Substances like glycerin, urea, lactic acid, and sorbitol, which attract and retain moisture in the skin. Natural Moisturizing Factors (NMFs): Low molecular weight compounds such as ammonia, amino acids, glucosamine, creatinine, citrate, and ionic solutions containing sodium, potassium, chloride, phosphate, calcium, and magnesium. Emollients: Ingredients like lanolin, one of the earliest complex organic substances used in facial and body moisturizers, which is derived from wool. Lanolin acts as a barrier to water loss (occlusive effect) and softens the stratum corneum by lubricating and smoothing the skin. Other emollients may include oil-water emulsions with various esters and oils, such as octyldodecanol, hexyl decanol, oleyl alcohol, decyl oleate, isopropyl stearate, isopropyl palmitate, isopropyl myristate, hexyl laurate, and dioctyl cyclohexane. Emulsifiers, Preservatives, and Fragrance Agents: These are also commonly included in commercial preparations to stabilize the product, extend its shelf life, and enhance its sensory appeal. Moisturizers are among the most frequently used and prescribed skincare products. However, the cosmetics industry often makes exaggerated claims about their effects, many of which lack scientific substantiation. Physicians, cosmeticians, and consumers should be well-informed about the actual science behind skin moisturization to understand what these products can and cannot achieve. In some cases, moisturizers may inadvertently increase dehydration, particularly when used near sensitive areas such as the eyes, lips, and genitals. These effects may be more pronounced in certain individuals. Additionally, the inclusion of plant extracts, certain alcohols, and proteins in moisturizers can heighten the risk of adverse reactions. To ensure safety and transparency, both cosmetic and therapeutic moisturizers should include a printed formula on their packaging. This allows consumers and healthcare professionals to identify potentially problematic components quickly and accurately.
